title: Johns Hopkins University Study Abroad Experience
paragraphs: I did clerkships in oncology, neurology and hematology at Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore, Maryland, in the United States. I sincerely thank everyone who supported me for the precious opportunity I was given. It was the most fruitful three months of my life so far, during which I studied absorbed, begrudging even my sleep.

On March 19, 2013, I landed in NY together with 王, who was studying abroad with me, and on the 20th I took Amtrak, a high-speed train, for two and a half hours and at last arrived in Baltimore. My first time on the East Coast of the United States, and my first time living alone! Looking up at the dome, the symbol of Hopkins, full of the weight of history and solemnity, and the colorful brand-new hospital building completed just last year, my heart leapt. I resolved to absorb as much as I could and grow before returning to Japan.

At Hopkins I met doctors and patients from all over the world. Their upbringings and the stories of how they came to Hopkins were each interesting, and I felt that the world is wide. When I talked with such people, there was only a relationship between people, and I felt there were no national borders. In the clerkships I sometimes worked with doctors who came from various countries such as India, China, Egypt, Panama and Nepal and had obtained their medical licenses in the United States. It is a world where ability decides, yet I thought it was personality and humor that attracted people.

The clerkship started with oncology. The day began with checking the charts of my assigned inpatients early in the morning and checking what had happened overnight with the night-shift doctor and the nurses. After checking, I examined the patients, worked out the Assessment and Plan from the findings, and prepared the chart. Because it is not an attending-physician-per-patient system, the residents are in charge of all the inpatients on the floor, and before 9 o'clock the team rounds began, joined by the attending and the fellow. Here I presented to the seniors and examined the patients together with them.

In presentations it is important to present concisely, in the set format but without missing the key points. The student is expected to understand the patient's condition better than anyone else on the team and to make a better plan by referring to papers and Up To Date. After the presentation there is a thorough discussion with members of other professions such as nurses, pharmacists, social workers and palliative care specialists. At first I was fully occupied just preparing the presentation, but when the attending pointed out specific antibiotic doses, side effects, fluids and so on, I was able to absorb new things and gradually became able to speak up in the discussions too. As differences from Japan, I think one can name always being conscious of the discharge goal and not keeping patients in hospital longer than necessary, and always confirming at admission whether resuscitation is wanted in an emergency. I got the impression that many patients understood their own condition and were eager about treatment. The doctors too devote themselves to treatment in cooperation with specialists in each field in order to respond to that wish. The expectations of those who have come to Hopkins seeking the best treatment are high, and I remember how, when the discharge was decided, one patient said with a radiant smile, "You were really wonderful doctors, and I am so grateful. Next time let's meet at a shopping mall or the beach, not the hospital!" I felt that a doctor's mission and the joy of working lie in this kind of thing. Being invited to the home of one of my assigned patients and enjoying a BBQ and the pool with their lovely children is also one of my warm memories.

Next I did a clerkship in the Hopkins neurology department, which was ranked No. 1 in the United States, and since I had wanted to do a clerkship there, I was very fortunate to be able to touch the world's top and see the differences from Japanese medicine. For three weeks I belonged to the general team and learned how to elicit findings and how to interpret them, and I experienced interesting cases such as paraneoplastic syndrome, cysticercosis, tuberculous meningitis, Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease, AIDS encephalopathy and conversion disorder. I was also given many opportunities to present on diseases, and I continued days of wrestling with papers while cutting into my sleep. For the remaining week I was on the stroke team and learned post-stroke management and diagnostic imaging. At Hopkins students work in the same way as residents. If you blend into the team and are trusted as a work colleague, you receive enthusiastic instruction and are entrusted with work. Starting with helping with examinations and procedures, for example when obtaining information on a new patient, I wrote the information release forms, got the patient's signature, phoned another hospital to have the chart faxed, and chose information from the thick chart to report to the resident, and so the work I could do on my own initiative gradually increased and I could feel myself moving forward little by little. Also, perhaps because the students entered medical school after graduating from university, they did their clerkships and studied intensively with a strategic view of their futures, which was a great stimulus. They read through textbooks and papers in their free time, and I was overwhelmed by their sharp ability to reason about cases. Although they had astonishing backgrounds, such as having come from Harvard or being former Olympic athletes, they did not show it, and they were very friendly and kind, even looking over my chart, and it was a very good experience to be able to study together in the same field with such students.

In hematology in the third month, I was in charge of consults in addition to inpatients. I was able to learn the difficulty of searching for the best treatment in situations with no correct answer, and the importance of not only applying the knowledge one has but also constantly accessing the latest information and incorporating it into daily practice. In hematology I acquired the habit of resolving questions not from textbooks but from Up To Date and papers. I was also introduced every time to the papers that served as the basis for treatment choices, and was surprised that the doctors constantly read papers and remember the important ones.

As for my English, I feel I grew a great deal in an environment where I was expected to perform at the same level as the local students. There is no special treatment as a "Japanese person" or an "exchange student." I realized that English is merely a tool for communication and what matters is what you say. At first there were times when I could not follow what was being said because of my lack of listening ability and medical knowledge. Also, I was slow even at reading a single paper and sometimes felt frustrated. However, I changed my mindset and, in order to approach a level at which I could discuss medicine, I recorded the conversation on rounds and did dictation at home to learn English expressions. I also printed the charts of patients other than my assigned ones to grasp the problems and treatments currently being addressed, and as a result I answered and asked questions more often on rounds, and I think my understanding deepened considerably.

Through this study abroad, coming into contact with the attending physicians' attitude toward work was a good opportunity to picture my future vision. The sight of them performing their work with vitality was dazzling, and the residents, while handling the hard schedule of night duty every four days, valued time with their husbands and children. And I was taught the wonder of a doctor's life: staying close to patients and being loved by them, and continuing to grow by mastering one's specialty. I was also able to meet doctors I wanted to take as role models, friends, nurses, assigned patients who were fond of me, and a roommate who made me laugh, and these encounters have become treasures.

Before studying abroad, the clerkship at Hopkins, the top in the United States, looked like an endlessly high mountain, but when I actually climbed it, a vast landscape spread out before me, and I was able to calmly see the respective strengths of Japanese and American medicine. I deeply thank Dr. 粕谷, who gave me this wonderful opportunity, everyone in the International Collaboration Office, and the professors of Nagoya University who have guided me this far. And supported by the kindness of everyone in the study-abroad group who cheered me up through the computer, my friends in the clinical clerkship group, and my father and mother who quietly pushed me forward, I was able to carry out a fulfilling clerkship. From next spring my year as a resident will begin, and I intend to make efforts with a broad perspective without forgetting what I experienced this time. Thank you very much.
